newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis, Palestinians clash over Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Israelis, Palestinians clash over Jerusalem.

text.p: Violence flared in the West Bank on Thursday over Israeli settlement building in Arab East Jerusalem and Jewish settlers opened a new front by moving into an Arab neighbourhood of the city.

Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu offered to finish making peace in six months but Palestinians called it a "publicity stunt" to avoid the world's condemnation for breaking ground this week on a Jewish settlement.
Israeli troops fired teargas at hundreds of Palestinian demonstrators in Bethlehem near Jerusalem.

Witnesses said protesters broke through about 40 Palestinian policemen to hurl stones at Israeli troops guarding the tomb of the biblical Rachel. Soldiers fired teargas from behind barricades and a few people were overcome by fumes.

Bulldozers dug for a third day into a hillside at Jerusalem's outskirts slated for the new Jewish settlement, while five settler families moved under cover of darkness into a sprawling house in the Arab Silwan neighbourhood.

Since 1991 at least 18 settler families have moved into Silwan, home to 30,000 Palestinians, an area just below the Old City walls where they say the biblical King David had the first capital of the Jewish people.
"This whole hill is part of ancient Jerusalem and our organisation's goal is for the whole hill to become Jewish," said Yigal Canaan, a spokesman for the El Ad settlers group.

Netanyahu's office said a settler leader had informed him of the entry into Silwan on Thursday but an official statement said the government did not initiate the action. It said Netanyahu had been reassured the settlement was legal.

A spokesman for the National Religious Party, the government's biggest champion of settlements, denied any significance to the timing so soon after the world condemned the groundbreaking for the 6,500-unit project for Jews on a hill the Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim and the Israelis call Har Homa.

Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East War and annexed it to the Jewish West Jerusalem as part of its "eternal" capital, although few states recognise the annexation. Palestinians regard East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state and consider the settlers a provocation.

Israeli security officials had predicted unrest following the groundbreaking on Tuesday, and Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said army intelligence suggested the Palestinians would turn to violence during weekly Friday prayers.

Aides to Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat slammed the offer by Netanyahu, which emerged on Wednesday, to accelerate peace moves and called it a trick aimed at scrapping existing deals that call for three West Bank withdrawals of Israeli troops.
"We are speaking of a publicity stunt," Arafat's adviser Ahmed Tibi told Israel Radio. "This is a strategic proposal whose aim is to wipe out the interim agreement completely."
Arafat, who had appealed to Palestinians not to let protests turn violent, left Gaza for Cairo on Thursday for talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on the crisis.
Mubarak was anchoring crisis talks also with Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara and Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri. Israeli planes bombed a guerrilla site in Lebanon in the morning.
Israel said Netanyahu would likely send foreign policy adviser Dore Gold to Egypt.

Clashes last September over Israel's opening of a tunnel near Islam's holiest shrine in Jerusalem evolved into gun battles between Israeli soldiers and PLO security forces in which 61 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers died.
